title: Ethiopian Grand Fasting Feast
community: All of Ethiopia — the expanded fasting platter
author: Mama Tigist
desc: Ethiopian Grand Fasting Feast — the expanded beyaynetu with all 10 preparations: Misir Wat, Shiro Wat, Kik Alicha, Kik Wat, Shimbra Wat, Gomen, Tikil Gomen, Fasolia, Duba Wat, and Hamli Wat on a vast communal injera. Ethiopia's greatest vegan feast — made for the most important fasting celebrations.
longDesc: The Grand Fasting Feast is the Ethiopian church celebration feast during major fasting periods — the most elaborate plant-based meal spread in Africa. The beyaynetu expanded to 10 preparations demonstrates that fasting food is not deprivation but abundance, not restriction but creativity.
steps: Two days before: make all five wats (Misir, Shiro, Kik Alicha, Kik Wat, Shimbra). All improve overnight.
Day before: prepare Gomen and Tikil Gomen. Prepare Duba and Hamli Wat.
Day of: warm all wats. Make Fasolia fresh.
Assemble the grand injera: arrange by colour — red wats, golden wats, greens, and vegetables in alternating sections.
chefTips: The grand fasting feast requires 2—3 days of preparation.
Colour arrangement is as important as flavour — the visual impact is part of the feast.
Everything improves overnight — the oldest preparation will be the most flavourful.
sustainabilityTips: The Grand Fasting Feast is 100% plant-based and provides complete nutrition. It represents one of the world's most ecologically sustainable feast traditions.
healthBenefits: The grand fasting feast is nutritionally perfect — providing complete protein from multiple legume combinations, all vitamins from the diverse vegetables, and extraordinary antioxidants from berbere. It may be the most nutritionally complete single meal tradition in the world.
culturalNote: The Ethiopian Grand Fasting Feast is one of humanity's most important food traditions — a 2,000-year-old completely vegan feast of extraordinary nutritional completeness, prepared by an Orthodox Christian majority not out of environmental philosophy but out of religious devotion, and that happens to be one of the greatest meals on earth. To sit before this feast is to understand that Ethiopian fasting is not about deprivation but about the transformation of simplicity into magnificence.
